tagline.text: Bicol's white sand beach where the stars come out instead of the lights

items.credit: Monette Nyem / CC BY 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The Calaguas island group off the coast of Camarines Norte is famous for Mahabang Buhangin, a beach as fine as flour. With little electricity or amenities, camping under a tent while listening to the waves and watching the Milky Way gives travelers who love camping and off-the-grid beaches an unforgettable experience.
The Calaguas group is a cluster of around 17 islands and islets on the Pacific, about
30km

off the coast of Camarines Norte in southeastern Luzon. Most belong to the municipality of Vinzons, and the one travelers visit is almost always Mahabang Buhangin ("long sand") on Tinaga Island. As the name suggests, the nearly
1km
stretch of white sand is as fine as flour, and behind the beach a gentle grass-covered hill rises, giving it a feel much like Korean grasslands.

This island was long called "Boracay's old self" because it has barely been developed. With no power grid, nights rely entirely on generators and solar lighting, and lodging centers on beach tents and simple huts. As visitor numbers have grown recently, hut-style resorts, paid showers, paid charging services, and even satellite internet in some areas have appeared, but there are still no big hotels or shopping streets.

On clear nights there is almost no light pollution, so you can see the Milky Way and a sky full of stars, and in the morning you can climb the hill behind the beach to watch the sun rise from the sea. Getting there takes several changes of bus, tricycle, and bangka and isn't easy, but for anyone who can enjoy the journey itself as part of the trip, this ranks among Luzon's finest beaches.

It suits young travelers who enjoy camping, groups of friends, and travelers who want to spend a whole day doing nothing on a quiet beach. It doesn't suit travelers who need air conditioning and hot showers.
Sand soft enough to sink your feet into stretches the length of the beach. The shallower water at low tide is good for swimming, and the water shines brightest in the afternoon.
Climb the grassy hill behind the beach for about
15–30 minutes
and the beach and surrounding islands come into view all at once. Leave around
, before sunrise, to catch the sun rising over the sea.
Pitching a tent and falling asleep to the sound of the waves is the core experience of Calaguas. On moonless nights, the Milky Way appears sharp and clear.
Charter a bangka to explore nearby deserted-island beaches, snorkeling spots, and rocky cliff coastlines. It's best to head out in the morning on calm-wave days.
Fish, squid, and pork bought at the Vinzons market are grilled by the boatman or hut owner. Eating barbecue on the beach at sunset is the highlight of a Calaguas trip.
You can rent a kayak or snorkel in the shallow water in front of the beach. The coral patches aren't large, but the clear water makes it easy to spot small tropical fish.

DLTB, Philtranco, Superlines, and other operators run daily buses from terminals in Cubao, Pasay, and Buendia in Manila to Daet, taking about
7–10 hours
for around
. An overnight bus lets you arrive at dawn and catch the morning boat the same day. From Daet to Vinzons it's about
30 minutes–1 hour
by jeepney or van, around
, and from downtown Vinzons to the port it's about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle.
The nearest commercial airport is Naga Airport (WNP), about
1 hour
from Manila. From downtown Naga to Daet takes about
2–3 hours

by bus or van, so flying doesn't cut much off the overall travel time. To save time, catch the first morning flight and take the same-day afternoon boat, or plan to stay one night in Daet — either is realistic.
A chartered bangka is the usual way from Vinzons port to Calaguas. A small 4–6 person boat costs about
round trip, and a large 15–20 person boat about
, with a one-way trip of about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes

. On busy weekends, shared bangkas sold by the seat are also available. The Paracale port route used to be common too, but the shorter Vinzons route is mainly used now. Using a travel agency's join tour (round-trip bus from Manila, boat, and tent included) makes preparation much simpler.
Calaguas is exposed to the Pacific, so sea conditions vary greatly by season. The best time is from
March
to
June

, when winds are light and the sea is calm, making boat travel comfortable and the water at its clearest. During weekends and Holy Week in this period, local campers crowd in heavily, so a weekday visit is recommended.
From
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon Amihan causes high waves that frequently suspend bangka service, and the coast guard often bans departures. From
July
to
October
is the rainy and typhoon season, with frequent typhoons passing through Bicol, making it hard to plan a trip.
The beach has almost no shade, so the midday heat index is very high. Sun exposure is especially strong from April to
May
, so bringing a tarp or shade canopy makes staying much more comfortable.

On-island lodging falls into three broad types. The first is beach camping — bring your own tent and pay only a site fee, or rent a tent on the spot. The second is nipa huts and small resorts behind the beach, with rooms equipped with a fan or a simple mattress at about

per night. The third is a group camp included in a travel agency package, with meals, tents, and the boat all bundled together, which is convenient for first-timers. On the night before or after, it's best to stay at a hotel in downtown Daet (about
per night).

The island has small shops and huts selling meals, but choices are limited and prices are higher than on the mainland. So most people buy fish, squid, pork, rice, fruit, water, and ice at the Vinzons market before heading in. Give the boatman or hut owner a tip and they'll cook the rice and grill the meat for you. Camarines Norte is known for its small, sweet Formosa pineapples, well worth trying. In Daet, you can eat Bicolano dishes like Bicol Express and laing cheaply.
There are no ATMs on the island, and cards are almost never used. Withdraw all the cash you'll need in Daet and bring plenty of small bills.
With no power grid, charging depends on paid generators or solar chargers. It's a good idea to bring two or more high-capacity power banks.
Phone signal only reaches weakly at some spots on the beach. It's a good idea to let family know your itinerary in advance.
Plan on at least 3 liters of water per person per day; ice and a cooler make food storage much easier.
The beach has little shade, so bring a tarp, hat, rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
Pitch your tent well above the high-tide line, and use sand stakes or sandbags to guard against wind.
It's best to agree clearly before departure on whether the bangka fare is round trip, whether island hopping is included, and what time you'll return.
Sunrise photos are best taken on top of Tinaga hill, and Milky Way photos at the end of the beach away from any lights.
If high waves lead the coast guard to ban departures, you could be stranded on the island, so it's best to leave at least a day of buffer before your flight or any important schedule.
Always wear a life vest on the bangka, and never board an overloaded boat.
Waste disposal facilities are limited, so take back all the trash you bring in. It's best to avoid glass bottles on the beach.
There's almost no lighting at night, so a flashlight is needed when moving around the beach, and swimming in the sea at night after drinking must never be done.
Mosquitoes and sand flies are common, so bring insect repellent.
Environmental fee and island-entry rules are changed frequently by the Vinzons tourism authority, so check the latest notices before you go.
